What velveting is

Velveting is an English name for a set of Chinese techniques that prepare meat for a stir fry or the fryer: cut it small, marinate it, and often give it a short first cook in oil. There is no single recipe. Two separate things are going on, and it helps to keep them apart.
Tenderising: something changes the meat itself, so it holds on to its water and stays soft. This is the job of an alkali such as baking soda, and of salt.
Coating: something sits on the outside of the meat and takes the heat first. This is the job of starch and egg white.
Cut first. Thin slices across the grain, about 3 mm, or strips about 1 cm thick. An alkali only works on the surface, so the more surface there is, the more it does.
The alkaline route: baking soda

This part is established. Baking soda raises the pH on the surface of the meat, which makes it harder for the proteins to bond tightly to each other as they cook. Proteins that bond less squeeze out less water, so the meat stays tender and moist.
As a short soak (Cook's Illustrated):
1 teaspoon of baking soda to about 340 g (12 oz) of sliced chicken breast, dissolved in a little water.
15 minutes is enough. In their test, 45 minutes gave the same result: the reaction is fast and does not build over time.
Their test does not say whether to rinse. At this amount most cooks do, and then pat the meat dry, because leftover baking soda tastes soapy.
In the marinade, with no rinse (Chinese Cooking Demystified):
¼ teaspoon of baking soda to about 200 g of chicken, mixed in with the salt, starch and egg white below.
The amount is small enough to stay in the dish.
They do not soak and rinse at all, and do not think it is needed.
More is not better. Too much, or far too long, turns the surface mushy and leaves a taste.
Egg white: a coating, not a tenderiser

Egg white is alkaline, but only mildly: about pH 7.6 when the egg is laid, according to the American Egg Board, and higher as the egg ages. That is the reason it is often said to tenderise meat the way baking soda does. No source checked for this page shows that it does.
What the sources do agree on is that egg white and starch together make a soft coating around the meat.
The coating holds juices that would otherwise leak out and steam away, and it shields the meat from the full heat of the oil.
So use egg white for the coating, and baking soda if you want the meat itself tenderised. Treat "egg white tenderises because it is alkaline" as kitchen lore.
The mechanical route
Cutting across the grain shortens the muscle fibres, so there is less to chew through. This does more than anything else here, and costs nothing.
Beating the meat flat breaks fibres and connective tissue, and evens out the thickness so it cooks at the same rate throughout.

Massaging the marinade into the meat is traditional, and it does get the salt and alkali over every surface. No source checked for this page measures any tenderising from the massaging itself, so count that as lore too.
A working marinade
For about 200 g of sliced chicken, from Chinese Cooking Demystified. Mix it in and leave it for 15 minutes or so.
¼ teaspoon salt, which tenderises like a dry brine and works quickly on thin slices
¼ teaspoon baking soda
½ an egg white
2 teaspoons cornflour
about ½ tablespoon oil, added last, which keeps the pieces from sticking together
Pepper, soy sauce and Shaoxing wine are for flavour and can be left out.
Coating for deep frying
A stir fry stops at the marinade. For crisp fried chicken, such as salt and pepper chicken, the meat gets a dry coat as well. This is the method from the takeaway recipe this page replaces.
Season the sliced chicken and leave it for 10 minutes.
Dip it in flour, then in beaten egg, until the egg is used up.
Coat it well in flour again.
The first coat of flour gives the egg something to hold on to, and the second is the part that turns crisp.
Frying
Fry in two portions, not all at once. It is easier to keep the oil hot and to turn the pieces.
Fry each portion twice:
45 seconds on a medium high heat, to set the coating
about 2 minutes with the heat turned down, to cook the chicken through
out of the oil to rest for a few minutes
30 seconds more on a medium high heat, to crisp it
The rest is what makes the second fry work: moisture moves out from the middle to the coating, and the second fry drives it off.
For a stir fry there is no dry coat. Pass the marinated chicken through oil at up to about 150°C for 30 to 45 seconds, until it looks cooked, and add it back to the wok at the end.
Finishing as salt and pepper chicken
Fry minced garlic and chopped green chilli on a low heat for 30 seconds, then add diced onion and pepper and cook until the onion is soft.
Toss the fried chicken with Salt and Pepper Seasoning, add it to the pan, scatter over chopped spring onion and cover for 15 seconds.
Baking soda tenderises and the coating protects. They are two jobs, and a recipe can use either or both.

Sources: Cook's Illustrated, "Tenderizing Meat with a Baking Soda Solution", for the mechanism, the soak amounts and the timing test. Chinese Cooking Demystified, "A Guide to Velveting", for the marinade amounts and passing through oil. The egg white pH is the American Egg Board's figure.
The coating and double fry are from a takeaway salt and pepper chicken recipe of unknown origin.
